newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Aussie dlr ahead but hesitant for jobs data.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Aussie dlr ahead but hesitant for jobs data.

text.p: The Australian dollar clung to modest gains late Wednesday after recovering from key support, but the rally faltered far short of safe territory.

The currency started 1/4 cent ahead after a U.S. bounce and hopped as high as US$0.7923 on talk Japanese names were fishing with big orders. But actual buying proved modest and traders scrambled to take profits when selling emerged out of Hong Kong.

Further gains were whittled away by offers from Japanese trust banks until exporter buying provided support at US$0.7890. Traders expect the market to remain hesitant ahead of domestic jobs data Thursday which just might lead to a rate cut here.

By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar had found a temporary base at US$0.7895/00 after being forced back from US$0.7923, but was still up on Tuesday's late US$0.7874/79. This was the currency's 18th trading day in the US$0.7855/7965 range.

The story was much the same on the crosses where it faded to 87.97/07 yen from an early 88.41 peak, but was again up on Tuesday's late 87.49/59. In trade weighted terms it ended at 58.5 from a previous 58.2 close.
Traders said early Japanese demand, likely related to another A$-denominated dual currency samurai issue, was curbed by a setback in US$/yen.
The currency had been on the rise after rumours influential Ministry of Finance official Eisuke Sakakibara had said U.S. officials told him they could tolerate the dollar at 120 yen.
But Sakakibara punctured the bubble saying the talk was groundless and the dollar eased to 111.30/35 yen from 111.70.

Nevertheless, the third samurai issue this week -- a 21 billion yen issue from Denmark -- stirred hopes Japanese demand was reviving now that the weak September U.S. payrolls report had diminished the chance of a U.S. rate hike.
Any revival could be short lived, however, given the real possibility of a cut in domestic rates before year end.

Many anlaysts think the Reserve Bank board will wait for Q3 consumer prices and wages data on October 23/24 to see if they confirm the downward trend in price pressures, and then sanction a 0.5 point cut at the next meeting on November 5.
But dealers cautioned that speculation of an earlier move would surely grow if the Thursday's September labour report proved much weaker than expected.

Median expectations are that employment will fall by around 7,500 in a modest payback for August's stronger than expected 37,900 rise. The unemployment rate, strangely, is seen easing to 8.6 percent from 8.8 percent on a lower participation rate.
The only data of note today were private sector credit which showed lending growth slowed to 0.3 percent in August after a very strong 1.6 percent gain in July.
Analysts noted annual growth remained a healthy 12.8 percent, suggesting the economy continued to cruise at a comfortable speed.
The breakdown showed personal lending remained robust with a 1.0 percent rise following July's hefty 2.8 percent jump, while borrowing for housing was running at a moderate 0.7 percent.
Business borrowing, however, eased by 0.1 percent after climbing 1.8 percent the month before.
That was the first monthly fall since September 1994 and cast some doubt on whether the government's high hopes for business investment in 1996/97 would be fulfilled.
In annual terms business lending was still up 15.7 percent.
Also due Thursday are housing finance commitments for August which were expected to dip by 1.5 percent as a payback for July's huge 16.0 percent jump.

That leap had preceded the cut in official rates on July 31 and analysts were keen to see if the easing had kept demand flowing, in what could be a turning point for the long depressed housing market. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
